activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
story:
The ice was bad at Practice Palace on Tuesday nights, chewed up by the afternoon public skate, and Alyssa dragged a puck through the ruts at center while twelve twelve-year-olds banged their sticks against the boards. She was eighteen, three weeks out of high school, and the association had given her the Bantam house team because nobody else wanted Tuesday nights. Her problem was simple and specific: in Saturday's game, forty-one pass attempts, seventeen completed, and every failed one she had watched on her phone in the bleachers afterward had died the same way, on the blade of a defender's stick laid flat across the passing lane.

She blew the whistle and set up the first drill before the kids could start maligning each other's mothers. Three lines, a cone, a coach standing in the lane with her stick on the ice, a rule that the pass had to get through or the whole line restarted. "It's a game condition," she told them. "That's Maya. Maya is the other team." Maya, who was fifteen and helping for service hours, took her role seriously and tipped the first four passes away.

"Make it harder," Maya called after the tenth failure, peevish now, or pretending to be, because the kids were getting loud about it. "Coach, this is impossible."

Alyssa stood at the blue line with her clipboard and watched Devon, her smallest winger, try the same flat pass for the fifth time. Sweep the puck, watch it clip Maya's blade, skate to the back of the line with his chin down. The drill was hers, designed by her, and it wasn't fixing anything. She had planned it like she planned everything now, with spreadsheets, with completion percentages, with a laminated periodization chart she'd made at two in the morning because planning was the only part of coaching that felt like something she could actually control. Her father called her system a technocracy, half admiring and half worried, and she'd laughed, but the word had stuck to her.

Flashback: her own last season, the semifinal, and she remembered it not as a whole but as one shift. Two-one, four minutes left, her on the wall with the puck and a defender's stick stretched across the lane like a toll gate, and she had tried to force the pass through anyway because forcing it through was what she knew. Turnover, goal against, season over. In the handshake line the other coach, an old man with a scratched whistle, had said something to her she hadn't understood until later. "You tried to go through the stick. There's another direction." She'd thought he meant around the stick. She'd spent a year thinking he meant around it.

Now, on the bad Tuesday ice, she pulled a puck from the bucket and walked it out to the faceoff dot. She'd been watching NHL clips on her laptop since Sunday, looping the same three seconds, and there was a pass she'd seen a hundred times without seeing. She rolled her wrists, opened the blade, and floated the puck off the ice, not high, just off it, so it skimmed flat over the stick she'd laid down as a test and dropped onto the concrete beyond. She did it again. Again it lifted, sailed level, and settled flat on the other side.

"Everyone in," she said.

They gathered at the dot, breathing hard, and she demonstrated at half speed. "You see how it lifts it just off the ice? Watch." She rolled the pass over Maya's stick, and it landed flat, wobbling, on the tape of Devon's blade where he'd parked it as a target. "It's called a saucer pass," she said. "It flies over their stick and it lands on your blade. That's the whole point of it. It lands on the blade, not the ice."

She didn't fully understand the mechanics, wouldn't have claimed to. What she understood was the geometry, and geometry was enough: a lane that was closed at ice level was open two inches above it. She rebuilt the drill on the spot, crossing out her laminated sheet in green marker, and had Maya raise her stick blade flat and low like a real defender, and made each kid attempt five saucers before the line could move. Devon's first three went end over end and one nearly cleared the boards. His fourth skimmed over cleanly and died perfectly on the tape, and he made a sound like a kettle.

"They'll get it by Saturday," Maya said during the water break, which was less a prediction than a question.

"Maybe." Alyssa watched Devon trying to teach the wrist roll to a teammate who wasn't listening. "Or maybe it takes a month and we lose three more games learning it. I honestly don't know which."

"That bother you?"

"A little. It's not in the spreadsheet."

Maya laughed. The whistle was cold in Alyssa's hand. She looked at the clock, at the twelve kids, at the ruts and the buckets and the crossing-out on her clipboard, all of it hers. Then she raised the whistle toward her mouth and skated to the dot, dragging the puck with her, blade open.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
The marble stairs of city hall were slick from rain, and Keira took them carefully, the binder of her case pressed flat against her chest. Inside, the hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper. A security guard pointed her toward the council chamber, where the mock court would sit, and where her coach, Ms. Okafor, had already arranged the chairs into a semicircle.

"You're arguing both sides today," Ms. Okafor said, not looking up from her clipboard. "Petitioner first, then respondent. Twenty minutes to prepare the second after you finish the first."

Keira had known this was coming. Still, hearing it said plainly made her stomach tighten. The case was fictional but modeled on a real dispute: a student suspended for a speech delivered off campus that the school claimed disrupted the learning environment. Keira had spent three weeks building the petitioner's case, that the suspension violated the student's rights, and she had built it well. She had quotes, precedents, a closing line about the marketplace of ideas that always drew nods.

She set her bag down at the petitioner's table and began unpacking. Across the aisle, Tobias from Lincoln Prep spread out his own materials, glancing at her with the flat confidence of someone who had only ever argued one side of anything.

"Both sides," he said. "Rough."

"I asked for it," Keira said, which was mostly true.

The panel filed in: three lawyers from downtown firms, volunteers for the day, plus a judge from the county court who would preside. The judge called the session to order and invited the petitioner to begin. Keira stood, straightened her notes, and started the argument she had rehearsed until it ran without her.

"The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1791, says that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech," she said. "A public school is an arm of the state, and punishing a student for words spoken off campus is abridging that freedom in everything but name."

The middle panelist leaned forward. "Congress, counsel. The amendment says Congress. Does it reach a school principal at all?"

Keira had an answer ready, about incorporation, about the Fourteenth Amendment carrying the prohibition against the states. She gave it cleanly, and the panelist nodded, though not as if he were convinced. More as if he were filing her answer away for later, and that unsettled her more than a challenge would have.

She finished strong. The judge called a recess, and Keira sat at the respondent's table with twenty minutes to become her own opponent.

Here was the problem she had been avoiding for three weeks: she did not believe the school was right. Or she believed it was wrong about this student, in this case, but she had begun to suspect it was not wrong in principle, that a school might sometimes have to silence speech to keep other students able to learn at all. She had shoved the suspicion aside as a contrivance of the assignment, something invented to make her argue badly on purpose. Now the invention was the assignment, and she had to make it honest or fail at it.

She turned to a clean page. Congress shall make no law. The words were absolute in form, and yet everyone in that chamber, including her, accepted that they were not absolute in practice. The petitioner's case rested on that gap being small. The respondent's case had to rest on it being, in some places, unavoidable. She began writing the suspension rationale not as a defense of the principal's judgment but as the narrow question of who decides: a principal who sees the hallway the next morning, or a court that never will. It was not an argument that the speech deserved punishment. It was an argument about institutional competence, and it problematized her own earlier claim in a way she thought might actually be true.

The recess ended too fast. She stood for the respondent and heard herself begin, "The school's obligation runs to all of its students, including the ones the petitioner's client targeted." Her voice steadied as the structure held. The judge probed; the middle panelist asked whether her position made the First Amendment a dead letter in schools. She said no, that it meant schools had to justify themselves, that the amendment existed precisely to make justification necessary, and that this principal had done so. She believed the last part less than she said it, and she let the panel see the hesitation rather than bury it, because a lawyer who never hesitated sounded specious, and she had decided, somewhere in the twenty minutes, that sounding right was worth less than being careful.

Tobias argued a brief rebuttal, and then the panel withdrew to deliberate. Keira sat with her hands folded, listening to the radiator tick. She had argued that the school was wrong and that the school had the right to decide, and she could not yet say which claim was the floor of her actual belief and which was the argument built on top of it. Perhaps both. Perhaps the amendment's flat certainty and the school's messy morning-after could only be held together by accepting that they pulled against each other, permanently.

The panel returned. The judge announced that the panel had split, that on balance they scored the respondent's argument higher, and that Ms. Okafor would want to discuss what that meant. Keira gathered her papers, both sets of them, and slid them into one side of the binder. The judge stepped down from the bench on his way out and paused beside her table.

"Which one did you believe?" he asked.

"Both," Keira said. "Ask me again in four years."

story:
Sienna had been maligning the tutoring centre for three weeks before she set foot inside it, mostly to her brother, who had suggested it. "It smells like dry-erase markers and defeat," she told him, and he said, "You've never been in it," and she said that was exactly the point of having opinions. But here she was on a Tuesday evening at the long table by the window, homework spread in front of her like evidence, while a boy named Theo from her calculus class worked two seats down, ostentatiously not looking at her.

The problem on her sheet was a polynomial on a closed interval, and she was supposed to find where it reached its largest value. She had learned to take the derivative that afternoon from a worksheet, a strange little machine of a process: bring the power down, subtract one, repeat. She could do it now without her pen trembling. She set the derivative equal to zero, found a tidy critical point inside the interval, circled it, and sat back.

"I got 2.4 seconds," she announced, because her problem was about a thrown ball and its height, which the textbook insisted on calling h of t.

Theo leaned over without asking, which was the closest thing to an invitation he'd extended all week. "Did you check the endpoints?"

"Why would I? The derivative is zero there. That's the top. That's the whole point of the derivative."

He pulled his own quiz out of his bag, unfolded it, and laid it beside hers. At the top, in red pen, was a mark she had to squint at to believe. "Fifty-eight," she said. "Theo. You're better at this than me."

"I found the critical point," he said. "I circled it, same as you. There was an interval, from zero to six, and the answer was at six. On a closed interval, the biggest value can sit at an endpoint, where the derivative isn't zero at all. So the endpoints have to be checked too. I lost nine marks for skipping it."

She looked at her own circled 2.4 and felt the specific vertigo of a floor rearranging itself. She tried the values anyway, plugging the left end and the right end of her interval into the original function, and the right end beat her critical point by a margin that seemed, in the moment, almost rude. The ball's highest point within the window of time they'd given her was simply the last moment of the window, still climbing on its way out of the problem.

It reminded her of the summer she'd spent, at eleven, digging for arrowheads behind her grandmother's house. Her grandmother had said the good stuff was deeper, in an older stratum of the yard, and Sienna had dug one careful hole and found a single bottle cap and declared the yard empty. Her brother had then, with the serene cruelty of older brothers, dug a second hole three feet away and produced a hinge and half a horseshoe. The lesson had never been stated. It had just sat there in the dirt, horseshoe-shaped.

"This is the bottle cap thing," she told Theo.

"The what?"

"I stopped at the first place that looked like an answer." She erased her circle, which took longer than it should have because she'd pressed so hard, and drew a small table with three rows: left end, critical point, right end. She filled it in. The right end won. She boxed that instead.

At the next table, a group of eighth graders was being obstreperous about fractions, loudly and in unison, and the tutor on duty, a graduate student named Priya, came over and confiscated a rubber band without breaking stride. She paused at Sienna's page. "Better," she said, and moved on, and Sienna found she was absurdly pleased with one syllable.

"So we're study partners now," Theo said. He said it to the window, in the tone of someone pretending to be casual about something already decided, and Sienna understood that this had been the point of the whole evening, the quiz laid out like a gift, the leaning over, all of it, and that neither of them was going to say so directly, because they were seventeen and this was the currency they traded in.

She still wasn't certain the derivative was anything more than a trick the textbook let her perform, a set of rules she could follow without trusting. But the table with three rows felt like something she could believe in: all the places an answer might hide, checked, none of them taken on faith.

"Only if you carry the pencil case," she said, and snapped it shut on his protest.

story:
Jasmine spread the printout on the picnic table and weighted its corners with her grandmother's teacups, which was a mistake, because the table still held last night's rain in shallow pools and the paper drank them at once, blooming gray along the edges. The assignment was due Monday: a formal critique of one painting, color, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings about the artist's life, just the object itself. She had chosen Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, 1940, mostly because it was the only reproduction in the textbook she could look at for longer than a minute without getting bored. Now, three sentences into her draft, she understood she had nothing.

Her grandmother came out with a dish towel over one shoulder and stood at her elbow, squinting down. "That's the one with the monkey," she said.

"And the cat. And the thorns. And that bird." Jasmine pointed at the small dark shape suspended at the painter's throat, its wings folded, its body slack. "I keep calling it ominous. Like a memento mori, a little death worn as jewelry. But my professor crossed that out on the practice paragraph. She wrote, where's your evidence, what does the tradition say?"

"What tradition?"

"That's the problem. There might not be one. It might just be decoration, something strange to hang there so the painting unsettles you."

Her grandmother lifted the teacup off the top corner and studied the wet page the way she studied lottery tickets, with a patience Jasmine had never managed. Then she laughed, one short note, as if the painting had told a joke only she had caught. "A dead hummingbird at the throat. In Mexico, that's a folk charm for luck in love. Young girls used to wear them."

Jasmine did not write it down immediately, because it seemed too easy, like finding the answer in the back of the book. But the fact settled into her the way sedimentary layers settle, one grain at a time, until the whole picture had a different weight. The hummingbird was not a symbol of death. It was a symbol of hope, dead in itself, and that was stranger than anything she had invented. She got her notebook and wrote it down in her worst handwriting so she would not lose it.

"Say that again," she said. "Exactly."

"A dead hummingbird is a charm. For luck in love." Her grandmother set the teacup back on the corner of the printout and went inside, leaving Jasmine with the sentence and the smell of the towel's detergent fading off the air.

She worked until the shade of the fig tree crossed the table, which was her private clock. The thorns made a new argument now. If the bird was a charm for love, then the thorn necklace that held it drew blood from the very neck where the charm hung, and the composition put both at the center of the canvas, framed by the lurking monkey on one shoulder and the black cat on the other, watchfulness flanking desire. The colors she had dismissed as simply gloomy, the dense green background foliage, the cooler green of the leaves strung through the thorns, formed a symbiosis of sorts: the jungle behind her and the jungle she wore were nearly the same green, so that she seemed to grow out of what imprisoned her. Jasmine wrote that down, then crossed out imprisoned, then wrote it again, because sometimes the obvious word was the true one and the student's job was not to avoid it but to earn it.

She drafted the whole critique at the picnic table, reading each paragraph aloud in a low voice to test whether it sounded like analysis or like showing off. The distinction kept sliding. When she wrote that the charm's hope and the thorns' violence formed a single ornament, she could hear her professor asking, but what does the artist believe about that, and Jasmine did not know. Maybe the painting held both without choosing. Maybe a woman could wear luck and blood at once and refuse to tell you which one she trusted.

By the time the mosquitoes came out, she had six paragraphs and a conclusion she half trusted, the kind that ended on a question. It felt dishonest to hide the uncertainty, and dishonester to pretend she had resolved it. She clipped the pages together, stacked the teacups, and carried everything inside, where her grandmother was still at the sink.

"Do I get to read it?" her grandmother asked, drying her hands.

"You'd read the part about the bird and say I plagiarized your brain."

"Then cite me," her grandmother said, and tapped the stack of pages with one wet finger. "Grandmother, personal communication."

story:
The tip jar on the counter read fifty-three dollars, which was close enough to the price of the crash cymbal Zachary had been circling online for six weeks. He had done the arithmetic so many times it had worn a groove in his head: nine dollars an hour, Saturdays and two afternoons, four more weekends if nobody called in sick. He wiped the espresso machine and watched the door for customers while his manager, Denny, restocked cups in the back with the dour efficiency of a man who believed joy was a form of theft.

Priya came in at noon for her shift, still wearing the lanyard from a university open house she had driven to that morning. She dropped her folder on the counter and pulled out a glossy brochure with a quad on it, lawns impossibly green. "It was good," she said, "except the money part. There was this girl ahead of me at the financial aid table, arguing with her dad. She kept saying tuition wasn't even the real number." Zachary poured her a house coffee, which was against the rules but which he did anyway, and asked what the real number was. "She said economists count the wages you give up while you're studying full-time as part of the cost of college, right along with tuition. So it's the tuition plus everything she could have earned if she'd just gotten a job instead." Priya shrugged. "Her dad called it crazy. She called it obvious."

Zachary thought about that while he steamed milk for a woman who took her latte to the window seat. It had not occurred to him that not earning money could itself cost money, that a paycheck you never received could sit in a column next to tuition like it was real. He turned it over the way he turned over a tricky fill pattern, slowly, with his hands waiting.

The trouble arrived at three, when Denny came out of the back and said the words Zachary had been dreading. "Saturday the eighteenth, I need you. Marcus quit, we're short, it's a double if you want it." A double was twelve hours. A double was the crash cymbal, the whole thing, in one day. Zachary said he would think about it, and Denny's face suggested that thinking was not what he was paying for.

The eighteenth was also the regional drum clinic an hour away, the one where a session player from a band Zachary actually listened to would take apart a groove and put it back together, and where, according to the flyer taped inside his locker, three music programs would have tables set up. He had dismissed it the moment he saw the date. Missing twelve hours of pay for a clinic felt like a luxury, the kind of thing people with savings did.

But Priya's open house girl had lodged something under his ribs. If the cost of one thing included the wages you gave up for it, then the cost of the double included the clinic, and the cost of the clinic included the double, and neither choice was free. He tried to instantiate the idea in his own vernacular: skip the clinic, buy the cymbal, keep the rhythm he already had. Take the clinic, keep the money in the jar, and hear something he couldn't yet play. It wasn't that one option cost something and the other didn't. It was that both of them cost, and you had to choose which cost you could live with. He still couldn't decide which was which. That was the part nobody's brochure covered.

He called his mother from the storeroom during his break. She didn't tell him what to do, which was her way of being merciless. "Which one do you still think about when you're doing the other?" she asked, and he said the clinic, and she said, "There's your answer, probably," and he said he hated the word probably, and she laughed at him. When he came back out, a man at the window seat asked for a refill and left five dollars in the jar, and Zachary watched the bills fold themselves over the coins and felt the arithmetic shift, and hated that too, a little, because it made the choosing harder rather than easier.

He told Denny at closing. "I can't do the eighteenth. I'm sorry. I'll take every other shift you'll give me." Denny stared at him for a long moment, then said, "Fine. Marcus is coming back anyway, he called this afternoon. Turns out his other job fell through." Zachary stood there holding the mop. He had spent two hours deciding, had laid two futures side by side and weighed them, and the whole thing had dissolved because somebody else's choice had changed the price of his. He laughed, once, before he could stop himself. "So you didn't need me anyway." "I always need you," Denny said, turning off the grinder. "Just not on Saturdays."

story:
Alex counted the cash in the envelope twice, then a third time, because the first two counts had not improved his opinion of them. Sixty-one dollars and change for eight hours of shepherding eight-year-olds through a slip-and-slide, which worked out to $7.25 an hour, the number printed on the flyer in the camp office window beside a cartoon sun wearing sunglasses.

His mother had said a job would teach him about the world. She had not specified which part.

On Friday, Marcus, who had worked at the camp the summer before, sat with him on the tailgate of the maintenance truck, both of them smelling of chlorine and juice boxes. Marcus pulled out his phone and showed Alex a photo of his cousin's paycheck stub from a camp across the state line, forty minutes east.

"Look at the rate," Marcus said. "Nine something an hour. Same job. Same kids, basically. Same bug spray."

Alex looked. His cousin DeShaun, whom he had met once at a barbecue, stood in the photo beside the stub like a man displaying evidence. The hourly rate was higher than his own, and the state on the stub was not theirs.

"That has to be fake," Alex said. "There's a minimum wage. It's a law. It's the same everywhere."

"It's real, though. He cashed it."

They took the problem to Priya, who ran the arts shed and was reading a paperback with a broken spine during her lunch. She listened with her sandwich halfway to her mouth.

"The federal minimum is $7.25," she said. "It hasn't changed since July 24, 2009. But states can set their own, higher ones."

"Since 2009," Alex said. "That's the year I learned to ride a bike."

"Congratulations to both of you," Priya said, and turned a page.

Alex spent the rest of the afternoon leading the yellow group in a game whose rules he invented as he went, which was more or less the job description. He thought about the border while a boy named Trevor accused another boy of looking at him. Forty minutes east, across a line he had crossed many times for mall trips without ever considering that the line might have a wage attached to it, DeShaun was earning more for the same whistle and the same chlorine. It offended some instinct of fairness Alex had not known he possessed until it was violated.

That evening he typed a message to DeShaun, deleted it, typed a shorter one, and sent it: how did you get the higher camp job. The reply came while Alex was washing the juice out of his shirt: they just posted it, man, I applied like you did. Which was both an answer and not one. DeShaun had not been cleverer. He had been closer.

The next week, Alex asked the camp director, a retired gym teacher named Carol who refereed disputes over popsicle distribution with judicial gravity, whether the camp had ever considered matching the other state's rate. Carol said the budget was the budget, and the budget was set by the township, and the township was not in the other state. Alex nodded as though this constituted information. Walking back across the field, he understood that he could quit and drive forty minutes east, and that the drive would eat some of the difference, and that he would be abandoning Trevor and the yellow group to whoever replaced him, who would be worse at the invented games. He also understood that staying was not a principle, exactly. It was inertia dressed up as loyalty, or loyalty dressed up as inertia, and he could not reliably tell which costume was which.

He stayed through July. On the last Friday, Marcus counted his own envelope on the same tailgate and said, "I'm applying over there next summer. It's not personal, it's geography." Alex said that sounded like something a T-shirt would say, and Marcus said he would put it on a T-shirt and sell it to both states at different prices. Trevor ran up holding a dead cicada like a coroner presenting findings, and both of them leaned in to admire it, and the dead cicada transfigured, in Trevor's telling, from a tragedy into a miracle of engineering. Alex, watching the boy's hands, decided he would apply east next summer too, and that he would also, in some arrangement he had not fully worked out, come back and visit. He put his envelope in his pocket without counting it.

"How much you got?" Marcus asked.

"The federal minimum," Alex said, "since 2009."

"That's so sad it's almost funny."

"Almost," Alex said, and Trevor held the cicada up to the light.

story:
The studio smelled of rosin and old coffee, and the window unit rattled whenever Ms. Okafor played anything below a low C. Henry sat with the guitar across his knee, his left hand still sore from three weeks of chords, watching her demonstrate a barre shape for the fourth time.

"You're strangling it," she said. "The neck is not a rival. Try again, gently."

He tried again. The F chord buzzed like a wasp trapped in a jar. His friend Dev had laughed at him on Tuesday, leaning against the lockers with the confidence of someone who had read exactly one book. "Malcolm Gladwell, 2008, Outliers," Dev had said, tapping his own temple. "The 10,000-hour rule. Ten thousand hours before you're any good. I'm seventeen already. It's mathematically over for us. You'd recuperate faster from a broken leg than you would from starting guitar this late."

Henry had gone home and done the arithmetic anyway, hunched over his desk with a pencil while his mother watched the news and muttered about stagflation, which apparently meant prices went up while everything else went down, a thing she considered personally offensive. Five hours a day for five and a half years. Two hours a day for thirteen. The numbers sat on the page like a verdict. He was sixteen. He had homework, a bus route, a life that was already full of things he hadn't chosen.

At the lesson he mentioned it, casually, tuning the low E as if the question were incidental. "So there's this idea. Ten thousand hours."

"Ah," Ms. Okafor said, and reached for the shelf behind the metronome. She pulled down a worn paperback with a cracked spine and dropped it beside him. Outliers, the cover said, and under the title, the author's name and the year, 2008. "Someone leaves this here every few years like a warning label. Page whatever-it-is." She went back to her own guitar and left him to it.

He found the chapter and read while she played scales, her part of the room sounding like water. The book did say it, more or less. Hours. Lots of them. But something in the phrasing made him pause, the way Gladwell kept leaning on the stories and smoothing over the footnotes, so that night he looked up the researcher the whole thing came from, a man named Ericsson. And there it was, plain as a bus schedule: Ericsson had said afterward that the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Not the total. The quality.

He thought about Dev, who had read the cover and the headline and considered himself informed. He thought about himself, who had done the arithmetic on a fixed number before checking whether the number was even the point. It occurred to him that he had been treating the 10,000 hours like a toll booth, exact change only, when Ericsson seemed to be describing something more like a diet, where eating ten thousand salads in a row would not save you if the salads were made of candy.

The next Tuesday Dev started in again at the lockers, calling it the putative death of Henry's musical career, which was a word Dev had learned for the SAT and now deployed on everything, putative snow day, putative pop quiz. Henry just said, "The guy who did the actual research said Gladwell missed the point. Quality over hours. Look it up." Dev looked taken aback, the way people do when a fact they own turns out to have a previous owner, and then, recovering, said, "Whatever. You still can't play an F chord," which was regrettably true.

That Thursday, at the lesson, Henry practiced the barre shape for forty minutes the new way, not repeating it blindly but stopping each time it buzzed, adjusting one finger, trying again. Ms. Okafor watched with the expression of a woman who had seen this exact scene many times and never tired of it. On the fifteenth attempt the chord came out clean, all six strings ringing together, and Henry sat very still, afraid to move his hand, as if the sound were a bird that had landed on him. Ms. Okafor nodded once and turned the metronome down to sixty. "Again," she said. "Slower this time."

story:
Raphael had come to his grandfather's house in late June with a textbook, a notebook, and the vague intention of getting ahead on calculus before orientation, though what he mostly wanted was to be somewhere that was not his mother's apartment, where every conversation curved back toward whether he had packed, whether he had called housing, whether he was sure about the loans. His grandfather lived at the end of a dirt road with a garden, a workshop, and a creek that ran through the back acreage under a wooden flume he had built himself decades ago. On the second morning, the old man stood at the window watching the water go through it and said, "I've been thinking about the throughput on that thing. It's not what it was."

"Throughput?" Raphael said, though he understood the word immediately; it had the flavor of engineering, of quantities per unit time, and it sat oddly in his grandfather's mouth, which usually produced only complaints about woodchucks.

"How much water moves through in a minute. I want to reroute some of it to the lower garden. But I have a fixed amount of pipe, so if I run the line one way I get more pressure and less distance, the other way more distance and less pressure." His grandfather turned from the window. "You're the one studying the mathematics now. Isn't there some method for this kind of thing?"

Raphael was honest enough to say that he thought there was, and unsure enough to add that he hadn't reached it yet. The textbook sat on the porch table all afternoon while he read ahead, past the sections he'd half understood in June, into a chapter on derivatives. The idea, as far as he could assemble it, was that a function rose and fell, and the derivative measured the slope at each point, and where the slope went to zero, the function had a peak. Somewhere in you could find the best of something, the most, the maximum, which was exactly what his grandfather was asking about with his pipe. He worked a practice problem and then another, and then messaged his friend Devon, because the notation was bothering him.

why does the book write the derivative like a fraction, he typed. dy over dx. it's not actually a fraction is it

Devon's reply came while Raphael was shelling peas on the porch. my cousin says it comes from Leibniz, he wrote it that way first, and it's still what everybody uses. nobody knows why it stuck, that's the joke. Raphael read it twice. He liked that a notation invented by one man, centuries back, had survived everyone who tried to replace it, and he liked less that he couldn't tell whether the fraction shape was a convenience or a truth. He looked at the dy/dx on his page, at the way it could be nudged algebraically as though it really were a numerator over a denominator, and decided provisionally to treat it as a notation that behaved well without committing to why. That felt like the kind of honesty his calculus teacher had proselytized about all spring, saying that knowing what you didn't know was the whole discipline, though Raphael suspected the man had mostly enjoyed the sound of it.

The next morning he set up the actual problem. His grandfather had sixty feet of pipe for the garden line, which had to run along two sides of the lower garden from the flume outlet, so the length of the run plus the width of the garden it served had to total sixty, and the area the line could irrigate was length times width. Raphael wrote the area as a function of the width, took the derivative using the rules he'd drilled, set it equal to zero, and found the width that made the area largest. He checked it twice. "Twenty by ten," he announced, carrying the notebook out to the workshop where his grandfather was cleaning a fitting in solvent. "Ten feet wide, twenty long, a hundred square feet of coverage. Anything else is worse. If you go twelve wide you lose area, if you go eight wide you lose area."

His grandfather dried his hands on a rag and took the notebook. He was quiet long enough that Raphael began to feel the boreal stillness of the place, the kind of northern silence that made him conscious of his own breathing. "Where's the dy over dx," the old man said finally. "This little symbol here."

"The derivative," Raphael said. "It comes from Leibniz. It's still the standard notation today." He found he liked saying it, liked tracing the lineage of the marks on his own page to a single hand.

"I know Leibniz," his grandfather said. "Calculating machine. Argued with Newton about who got there first and lost, mostly." He set the notebook down on the workbench, next to a coffee can of bolts. "Twenty by ten, you said. Come outside."

They walked down past the flume to the lower garden, where the old lines still lay half-buried, the previous system his grandfather had abandoned years ago when the pump at the well began failing. "Your grandmother measured that garden the summer before she died," his grandfather said. "She had a folding rule and a theory about sun. She moved the corner stakes four different times, one summer, trying to get the most out of it." He toed at a rusted stake still leaning at the garden's corner. "Twenty feet one way, ten the other. She never wrote an equation in her life. She just kept moving the stakes until nothing she did made it better."

Raphael stood looking at the stake, at the rectangle of weeded ground around it, holding his notebook with its careful derivative, its slope set to zero, its proof of optimality, and understanding that he had spent two days deriving what a woman with a folding rule had found by standing in the dirt. He did not feel foolish exactly. The equation could be reused on the next garden and the one after that, and her method could not be mailed to a stranger. But when his grandfather asked whether his answer was right, Raphael heard himself say, "It's the best possible one," and then, because he was tired of certainty he hadn't earned, "At least it's the best if the garden is a rectangle. If she'd wanted a circle, I'd have to start over."

"A circle," his grandfather said, and laughed, and began pulling the stake.

story:
The screen door banged behind Owen before he could catch it, and his grandfather looked up from the kitchen table where he was sorting receipts into piles. For two weeks of summer Owen had been assigned this house, this table, this laptop, and an online course whose second unit was titled Objects and Encapsulation. His grandfather, a retired accountant, had made the table available without questions, the way he made everything available.

"You're quiet up there," his grandfather said that morning, though Owen was five feet away. "Good quiet or bad quiet?"

"Test quiet," Owen said. "I wrote a class and a test for it, and the test says it failed, but I think it's lying."

His grandfather folded a receipt into its envelope. "In my line, when the numbers said one thing and I believed another, the numbers won eventually. Every time."

Owen turned back to the laptop. He had built a class called Vinyl, because his grandfather's record shelf ran the length of the living room wall and it was the first concrete thing in the room worth naming. He had made the fields private, the way the textbook insisted: a String for the title, an int for the year, a boolean for whether it was still in its shrink wrap. Then getters for each one, small public methods that handed the values out, and a constructor that set them. That part had felt almost ceremonious, like sealing something in a vault and then issuing a single key per door.

The test was the problem. He had written it the night before in the blue glow of the guest room: create a Vinyl, set the year to 1971 through the constructor, then call an assertEquals on the getter. When he ran it, the failure message told him it expected 0 and got 1971, which was backwards, which was insulting. He had not written 0 anywhere. He read the message four times, then closed the laptop and slept badly, dreaming in red failure bars.

He opened the test file again now. His grandfather came and stood behind him with a glass of iced tea, saying nothing, impervious in the way of a man who did not need to understand the screen in order to believe it could be understood. Owen read his own line aloud, slowly, the way he read poetry in English class when the sense kept sliding off. "Assert equals, zero comma, record dot get year." He stopped. He looked at the numbers in the message again: expected 0, got 1971. The 1971 had come from his getter, so his getter was the second thing in the line, the actual one. Which meant the first thing in the line, his zero, was what the framework called expected. He had put them in the wrong order. JUnit's assertEquals took the expected value first and the actual value second, and he had swapped them, and so the message reported his mistake back to him in a voice that made it sound like the code's mistake.

"Found something?" his grandfather asked.

"I called it wrong and it answered honestly anyway." He swapped the two arguments, year first, getter second, and ran the test. The bar at the top of the window turned green, a clean and total green, and he sat back and laughed once, short, at himself.

His grandfather pulled out the other chair. "You know, people used to denigrate that kind of machine, back when I started. Said it would make us careless. Never understood that. The machine was the careful one. Half my job was proving to clients I was as careful as the machine, that handling their money wasn't some game. A fiduciary, they call it. Someone who has to put your interest first and can't hide behind fine print."

"Like the fields," Owen said, surprising himself. "Private. They can't just be grabbed by anything that wants them. You have to go through the getter, the one door that's accountable." He was not sure the comparison held all the way down, and he said so. His grandfather shrugged, as if to say comparisons rarely did, and drank his tea.

That afternoon Owen wrote three more tests, each with the expected value first and the actual value second, and each one green on the first run. He failed one on purpose, just to watch the message, and this time the message named the right numbers in the right order. He left the failing version in a comment at the bottom of the file, a small monument to the night he had lost to it. Then he walked to the record shelf, found a 1971 pressing of an album with a worn corner, and carried it back to the table.

"This one's getting its own test," he said, and opened the laptop again.
